# Hard-to-vary report: the Time Traveller's argument (Chs. I–VI)

## 1. The question, frozen

The document answers several things; its opening ("the Time Traveller ... was expounding a recondite matter to us") makes one central: **why should time travel be possible at all** — the in-story case the Traveller lays out before any demonstration. Range: his speech in Ch. I–II. Kind of question: an *argument for a conclusion* (by-domain: Arguments), not a diagnosis or a proof. The tabletop demonstration and his own bedraggled return are evidence he offers *for* that argument, not separate explanations, and I treat them that way.

## 2. The explanation in parts (owner's words, paraphrased)

- **P1.** A durationless ("instantaneous") thing cannot be real; so any real thing needs Length, Breadth, Thickness, and Duration — four "directions."
- **P2.** Time is "only another way of looking at" Space; it differs from the other three only in that "our consciousness moves along it" one way.
- **P3.** We move freely in two spatial directions, are limited in the third by gravity, but have partly beaten that limit (balloons); by the same pattern we might beat our limit in time.
- **P4.** Consciousness already "travels" through time — steadily, cradle to grave — and even jumps back briefly in vivid memory.
- **P5.** Conclusion: a steerable machine should speed, slow, stop, or reverse this drift.
- **P6.** Corroboration: the model, watched under stated-controlled conditions, vanishes when the lever is pressed.
- **P7.** Patch (the Psychologist): if the model went into the past rather than the future, its absence on earlier Thursdays is explained by "presentation below the threshold" — a fast-moving thing looks too dim to see, like a spinning spoke or a flying bullet.

## 3. Part by part

| Part | Mark | Why |
|---|---|---|
| P1 (durationless things aren't real) | **Loose** | Swap it for simply asserting "duration is a fourth quality" and P2 onward are unaffected. It primes the listener to accept P2; nothing downstream depends on it. |
| P2 (time is a dimension, differing only in how we move along it) | **Held if** | Held only if "direction" already means "an axis traversable both ways" — which is the very thing being argued for. This is the conclusion showing up inside a premise (hunt-the-starting-points). The doubtful job it depends on: an independent reason duration is that kind of axis, which is never supplied. |
| P3 (gravity/balloon analogy) | **Loose** | Swap the balloon for a swimmer against a current or a climber against altitude: the passage reads the same. What's actually shared — "a present limit needn't be permanent" — is true of nearly anything and doesn't specifically back time travel. |
| P4 (memory as a "jump back") | **Loose**, doing less than claimed | Flip: vividly remembering an event is not being at it — nothing there responds if you poke it (you cannot touch anything in the recalled moment). Swap "recalling the past" for "imagining the future": equally persuasive, equally empty. A label, not a mechanism. |
| P5 (build a machine to steer the drift) | **Unknown** | Rests entirely on P1–P4, all loose or held-if. No part pins it down independently. |
| P6 (the vanishing model) | **Held if** | Held only if a hidden mechanism is ruled out. The text asserts "no trickery" but never tests it: no outside operator, no repeat with the Traveller not touching the apparatus. Poke test: a conjuring vanish and a genuine temporal disappearance look identical from where the guests sat, so this evidence doesn't discriminate. |
| P7 (presentation-below-threshold) | **Borrowed / catch-all, no gauge** | Leans on a real optical fact (a fast spoke blurs), but is wheeled in at the exact moment an objection (Filby's: "we'd have seen it on earlier Thursdays") needs answering, and nothing says what result would show "diluted presentation" to be wrong. |

## 4. Whole-explanation checks

- **Flip.** The same stock ("some limits have been beaten before") could just as well argue *against* hope: "some limits, like running time backward, never yield." "Why should he not hope" doesn't discriminate between a possibility-conclusion and its opposite.
- **Direction.** No test in the text separates P2 ("time is dimension-like, hence traversable") from the much plainer view "time is just an ordinary one-way parameter, no different from the physics everyone already accepts." At this level the two are the same explanation; the speech simply asserts the livelier one.
- **Answer hidden in starting points.** Yes — in P1→P2, as above.
- **Add a job.** No one asks "if consciousness already moves through time, why can't it also be sped up or reversed, the way the machine soon will be?" That job is never posed, so nothing rules out rivals that would fail it.
- **Catch-alls.** P7, ungauged, as above.
- **Build the best rival.** "He built a clever conjuring trick, and separately later had a rough physical ordeal of ordinary origin" fits every fact so far (the vanishing model, the muddy, injured return) exactly as well as "he time-travelled." Nothing in Ch. I–IV yet tells the two apart.
- **Provenance.** P1–P3 are *Asserted* (stated, not built or tested in the text). P2 is also *Borrowed* — it leans on real 1880s–90s four-dimensionalist popular science the text half-cites (Professor Newcomb), a background theory not itself under test here. P7 is *Asserted*, invoked once, ad hoc.

## 5. What would make it harder to vary

One independent poke on P6: someone other than the Traveller controls the lever, or the "vanished" object is checked for afterward by instrument, not eye. And one real added job for P2/P4: a prediction that follows from "time is dimension-like" but not from "time merely passes," which the text then actually checks. Either would stop the machine's central claim from resting on assertion and analogy alone.

## 6. What this does not show

None of this says Wells's premise is false or that the passage fails as fiction. Its job in the novel is to earn the reader's suspension of disbelief before the real story starts, not to survive a physicist's audit — and by that different job it may succeed completely (it plainly persuaded generations of readers). Hard-to-vary only tests the narrower claim that this speech *explains* why time travel should work; it says nothing about the passage's craft, and nothing about whether time travel is in fact possible.

## 7. One next step

Press on the single move carrying the most real weight — "consciousness already travels through time, so a vehicle might too" (P4→P5) — and ask what would have to be true of consciousness's "travel" for the analogy to transfer: could it be sped up, banked, or spent under any independently checkable condition? If nothing answers that, the whole conclusion leans on P6's unpoked demonstration alone.
